items.item: The 'static bound on thread::spawn is not about the closure itself living forever; it is about there being no borrow inside it with a lifetime the compiler could prove ends before the thread does

items.item: E0373's two sub-messages matter: 'may outlive the current function' names the risk, 'is borrowed here, which is owned by the current function' names exactly which value and why it's at risk

thread::scope's soundness doesn't come from a weaker rule; it comes from scope() itself being unable to return until every scoped thread has actually joined, which the type signature's 'scope lifetime encodes
A scope cannot help when a thread must genuinely outlive the function that spawned it, because the scope's own call would then also have to still be running — that's the case Arc solves instead

at.step: Needs to outlive the function? Clone an `Arc` instead

items.item: 'static is a property of a value's type (does it contain any reference shorter than the program's lifetime), never a property of control flow (whether or when a function returns)

tokio::spawn's lack of a scope equivalent isn't an oversight; it follows necessarily from the fact that a task can be dropped wholesale on shutdown, which thread::scope's join guarantee has no analogue for

The async_scope-guard thought experiment is exactly isomorphic to thread::scope's own soundness argument, which is what makes mem::forget defeating it so damning: the identical proof technique that works for threads fails for futures

at.step: Could a scoped async spawn ever be sound?

items.item: mem::forget being 100% safe is the load-bearing fact: if forgetting a Drop guard required unsafe, the soundness argument for an async scope would still hold, because unsafe code accepting responsibility is exactly how Rust tolerates few corners like this elsewhere

The fix for async is never 'add more unsafe'; it's the same two tools as threads minus the scope option: move owned data in, or move a reference-counted clone (Arc) in, so the spawned future never holds a borrow to begin with

items.item: Crates that offer scoped-looking async spawning exist but accept the unsafe risk explicitly somewhere internally; they don't contradict this topic's claim, they confirm it by needing to patch around the same gap
